title: Object-oriented, functional or service layer?

rows.label: In one line
values: Objects that own their data and the methods allowed to change it
Pure functions that turn immutable values into new values
Stateless services that run each use case over plain data objects

rows.label: Where state lives
values: Inside objects, in private fields changed only by their methods
In immutable values passed from function to function; real changes are pushed to the edges
In the database and in plain data objects loaded per request; services keep none

rows.label: Where behaviour lives
values: In methods on the object that owns the data
In standalone functions that take data and return data
In service methods, one per use case, between controllers and repositories

rows.label: How variation is handled
values: Several classes behind one interface, picked at run time (dynamic dispatch); subclasses, used sparingly
Pass a different function in; branch over the shapes a value can take
Inject a different implementation of an interface through the constructor

rows.label: Testing
values: Put the object into the right state, call methods, check the result; mock its collaborators
Call with inputs and compare the output; no setup and no mocks for the pure core
Pass fakes for repositories and gateways to the constructor

rows.label: Concurrency
values: Shared mutable objects need locks or must stay on one thread; Kay’s message-passing objects avoid that, like actors
Immutable data can be shared freely; parallel pipelines are safe when the functions are pure
Services hold nothing, so you run more copies; the database transaction handles conflicts

rows.label: Typical languages and frameworks
values: Java, C#, C++, Python, Smalltalk, TypeScript classes; Go’s interfaces without a type hierarchy
Haskell, OCaml, F#; the same style in JavaScript, Java streams, Rust iterators and React
Spring (`@Service`), NestJS (`@Injectable`), ASP.NET Core, Rails service objects

rows.label: Common failure mode
values: Deep inheritance trees and a noun for every verb (`AbstractProxyMediator`)
Dense chains nobody can read, hidden copying costs, effects leaking into “pure” code
All rules in fat services over bags of getters and setters (the anemic domain model)

rows.label: Pick it when
values: Long-lived things with rules to protect, and many variants behind one interface
Calculations, transformations and rules you want to test easily and run in parallel
Business backends with several entry points, on a framework that already expects it

tip: These aren’t rival camps; most real backends use all three. A common, healthy mix: a service layer as the entry point for each use case, domain objects that guard their own rules, and pure functions for the calculations in between. Reach for objects where state has rules, functions where data flows, and services where a request has to be coordinated across a database, payments and email.
